| [NOTE-029](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-029.md) | Krauska & Lau 2023, moving away from lexicalism | Standard production and comprehension models built on "lemmas" (stored triads of meaning, syntax and form, with syntax stopping at the word) inherit a lexicalist assumption that typology has refuted. Replacing that assumption needs new algorithms, not just new representations: separate meaning↔syntax and syntax↔form mappings with one integrated stage for retrieving and assembling syntactic structure. This predicts different aphasia profiles. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-065](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-065.md) | Bruening 2018, lexicalism: wrong and superfluous | The lexicalist hypothesis, that a separate, encapsulated component builds words before phrasal syntax, is wrong and superfluous. Phrasal syntax feeds word formation, phrasal operations reach inside words, and the two obey the same principles. The facts it was meant to explain have independent explanations that never mention "word", so grammar needs only one combinatorial component. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-073](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-073.md) | Haspelmath 2011, the indeterminacy of word segmentation | None of the ten standard criteria for a cross-linguistic "word" (pauses, free occurrence, mobility, uninterruptibility, non-selectivity, non-coordinatability, anaphoric islandhood, nonextractability, morphophonological idiosyncrasy, deviations from biuniqueness) is necessary and sufficient, and no combination reproduces orthographic practice. So linguistics has no principled basis for a universal morphology–syntax division, and morphosyntax should be treated as one domain. | Skimmed |
